interviewQuestions.question: What does it actually mean for an app to be 'offline-first,' and how is that different from just caching data for when the network is unavailable?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Offline-first means the local database is the app's real source of truth — every screen renders from it regardless of connectivity, and every write lands there first, always succeeding locally, full stop. The network's job shifts to keeping that local store in sync in the background, not being on the critical path of reads or writes.

That's a stronger claim than 'we cache data for offline use.' A cache-then-network app shows cached data instantly but still treats the network as primary — a write with no connection typically still fails outright, because writes were never rerouted through the local-first path. Offline-first apps decouple writes from connectivity entirely: adding an item to a cart, editing a note, or sending a message all succeed locally and instantly, with the actual sync to the server happening whenever connectivity allows, via a queue.

The concrete test I'd apply to tell them apart: turn off the device's network entirely and try to both read AND write. If reads work but writes fail, that's cache-then-network, not offline-first. If both work seamlessly and the user genuinely can't tell they're offline until they specifically check, that's offline-first.

**Testing:** whether you know this is a real architectural distinction with concrete behavioral differences, not just two names for the same caching idea.

interviewQuestions.question: Design the offline-first read/write path for a note-taking app where users frequently edit notes without connectivity.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The UI reads exclusively from a local database (SQLite, Core Data, Room, whatever fits the platform) — never directly from the network for rendering. Every edit writes to that local database immediately and the UI reflects it instantly, regardless of connectivity; there is no 'saving...' state gating the user from continuing to type.

For sync, I'd run a background process that watches for local changes (a dirty flag or a change log per note) and pushes them to the server whenever connectivity is available, and separately pulls remote changes down into the same local database. Because notes can be edited on two devices while both are offline, I'd need an explicit conflict strategy up front — depending on the product's actual requirements, that could be last-write-wins with a timestamp (simple, but silently drops one edit), or something field-level or CRDT-based for text if concurrent edits to the same note are common enough to matter (this is exactly what [Data Synchronization & Conflict Resolution](data-sync-conflict-resolution) covers in depth).

For connectivity loss mid-write, I'd queue the pending change (in a table, with a stable ID for the note and an idempotency key for the sync operation) rather than attempting the API call synchronously — that queue drains whenever the sync process detects connectivity, and each entry needs to survive an app restart before it's synced, since 'offline for three days then reopens the app' has to work identically to 'offline for three seconds.'

I'd surface sync status visibly — a small 'synced' / 'pending sync' indicator per note — so a user editing offline for an extended period isn't surprised later about what did or didn't make it to the server.

**Testing:** whether you can design the concrete read/write/queue/sync pieces together, not just describe the concept abstractly.

interviewQuestions.question: A user reports that after being offline for an hour and liking several posts, none of their likes actually registered once they came back online. How would you debug this?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My first hypothesis, given 'none registered,' is that the write queue either isn't persisting entries durably or isn't actually draining on reconnect — a total failure like this points at the queue mechanism itself rather than an individual sync bug, which would more likely show partial success.

I'd check a few specific things in order: is the queue backed by the actual local database (surviving process death) or held only in memory — an app backgrounded and killed by the OS during that hour would lose an in-memory queue silently, with no error surfaced to the user at all. Next, is there a listener actually watching for connectivity changes and triggering a drain, or does the queue only get processed on next app launch — if the user's app stayed in the foreground the whole time and connectivity came back without a relaunch, a launch-only drain trigger would explain exactly this symptom.

I'd also check whether the optimistic UI update (showing the heart filled) is disconnected from the actual queue write — if the 'like' button's local visual state isn't derived from the same underlying queued-operation record the sync engine reads, the UI can show success while nothing was actually queued for sync, which would explain why the user believed the likes registered until finding out otherwise.

Once isolated, the fix is either persisting the queue to the local database if it wasn't already, or wiring an actual connectivity-change listener to trigger a drain rather than relying on app launch timing.

**Testing:** whether you can systematically isolate a total-failure bug to the specific broken link in the queue/sync/UI chain rather than guessing at a single likely cause.

interviewQuestions.question: Would you build full offline-first support for a news-reading app where users mostly browse articles and occasionally bookmark one?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Probably not the full offline-first treatment — I'd separate what this app actually needs by read versus write behavior, because they have very different requirements here. Reading articles is exactly the case cache-then-network handles well: fetch and cache article content, show it instantly on repeat views, refresh in the background — full offline-first's added complexity (a write queue, conflict resolution, a sync engine) buys little for content that's fundamentally read-heavy and rarely edited by the user.

Bookmarking is the one write action in this product, and it's a good candidate for a lighter version of the same idea without the full sync-engine investment: write the bookmark to local storage immediately (so it feels instant and works offline), and sync it to the server opportunistically — a simple queued write with retry, not a full bidirectional sync engine with conflict resolution, since bookmarks are unlikely to be edited concurrently on two devices in a way that creates real conflicts worth resolving carefully.

I'd reserve genuine offline-first investment — the write queue, the conflict strategy, the sync engine — for products where offline **writing** is a core, frequent part of the product experience: a field-work app, a collaborative notes app, a chat client. For this news app, that investment doesn't match the actual usage pattern, and I'd rather ship a simpler cache-then-network read path plus a lightweight queued write for the one write action that exists.

**Testing:** whether you can right-size the architecture to the product's actual read/write pattern instead of defaulting to the most sophisticated pattern regardless of fit.
